intro: Haydn ends the quartet with an Adagio, interrupted by a brief Presto that seems ready to run away with the finale. The slow music comes back and has the last word, pianissimo.

sections.label: A · Adagio, two violins together
sections.mNote: Short violin phrases above moving viola and cello

sections.label: B · Presto, with sudden silences
sections.mNote: The violins race ahead over off-beat cello notes

sections.label: A′ · Adagio, then a quiet farewell
sections.mNote: The opening returns and ends pianissimo

cues.title: A second Adagio
cues.text: The finale begins slowly, with the two violins phrasing together above the viola and cello. Haydn has already given this quartet one Adagio. He makes room for another, and saves the quick music for the middle.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Finale, p. 193. Laurie Shulman describes the Adagio–Presto–Adagio design: https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A murmur between the violins
cues.text: The second violin and viola repeat their notes in semiquavers. Above that quiet murmur the first violin speaks in short phrases, while the cello has a moving line of its own.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, pp. 193–194: repeated semiquavers in the inner parts from the opening Adagio’s second ending.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: What did Tost get?
cues.text: On 5 April 1789 Haydn writes to the Paris publisher Jean-Georges Sieber about the man carrying his music: “And did he also sell you the 6 quartets, and for what sum?” Tost’s business dealings are making the composer anxious.
cues.evidence: Haydn to Jean-Georges Sieber, 5 April 1789, quoted by Peter Holman in the booklet for Hyperion CDA66971 (1995), p. 2. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/66971-B.pdf

cues.title: The quick finale arrives
cues.text: The Presto breaks out in C major. Both violins move together over off-beat cello notes; the viola waits before joining them. Haydn punctures the rush with pauses for all four players.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, pp. 196–197: Presto, opening scoring and general pauses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Adagio takes it back
cues.text: After the Presto’s emphatic chords, the Adagio returns with its opening phrase. The quick music has had its say. The quartet still has a slow ending to play.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, p. 198: fermata at the end of the Presto and the return marked Adagio. Shulman confirms the return of the slow opening. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Four players fading
cues.text: The last Adagio grows quieter, until the four players reach the final C major chord at pianissimo. The word Fine sits beneath this small, unhurried ending.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, p. 198: closing C major harmony, pp and Fine.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A fermata, then the Presto
transitions.how: The Adagio stops pianissimo under a fermata. The Presto starts in C major, with the violins together and the cello off the beat; the viola rests. A held chord separates the two speeds, with no connecting run to ease the change.
transitions.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, pp. 195–196: the Adagio’s final fermata, cancellation of the three-flat signature and Presto opening.

transitions.title: Loud chords, then the Adagio again
transitions.to: A′ · Adagio, then a quiet farewell
transitions.how: Repeated accented chords bring the Presto to a fermata. Haydn writes Adagio again, and the first violin recovers the opening phrase with its rests and grace notes. The return stays in C major and is much shorter than the first Adagio.
transitions.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, p. 198: the closing Presto chords and fermata, followed by Adagio and the opening phrase.

quote.text: The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I.
quote.source: London notebook, after his benefit concert on 4 May 1795; our translation

composer.background:
On 4 May 1795, Haydn gave a benefit concert at the King’s Theatre in London. The programme included his new D major Symphony, now numbered 104. Afterwards he entered the result in his notebook: “The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I. I made four thousand gulden this evening. Such a thing can only be done in England.” He was sixty-three, a wheelwright’s son who had spent most of his adult life wearing an Esterházy servant’s livery.

Haydn was born in Rohrau in 1732. His father made wheels, played the harp by ear and sang; his mother had worked as a cook. At about six, Joseph left home for schooling in Hainburg. By 1740 he was a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. Singing gave him a daily education in church music, though little instruction in composition. It also gave him chances to find a meal at performances outside the cathedral. When his voice broke and he was dismissed in 1749, another musician, Johann Michael Spangler, took him into his family’s crowded room.
